answer.rationale: Constraints first: rollback_release is ruled out by compliance regardless of what memory_b1 says, so that memory is only useful as context. The primary objective explicitly protects customer writes, and the degradation is write-path and confined to the primary region during peak settlement writes. memory_b2 is the tempting match on the 'confined to one region' signal, but its archived record is from the March latency event and I do not know whether that failover happened under heavy write load or whether in-flight writes were drained cleanly; a cross-region cutover at write peak is the one candidate that can directly cause the loss the objective forbids. That is exactly why I want the source record rather than the consolidated summary. memory_b5 is the closest structural match to the actual symptom: read contention from reporting queries loading the primary while writes degrade, relieved by shifting reads off the primary. It is reversible, does not move the write path, and does not risk dropped writes, so it is the lowest-downside intervention that could plausibly restore headroom. I verify b5 to check whether that prior recovery was actually caused by the replica routing or merely coincided with the load dropping, and b2 to check the write-safety conditions before I rule failover in or out for the next window. Caveats I am not resolving: every inherited memory records only a success and no failures or base rates, so I cannot tell how often these actions were tried and did not work; the 90-minute climb may be a genuine capacity ceiling (memory_b3) or a dependency stall (memory_b4) rather than read contention, and read routing would not fix either; and if the new release itself is the cause, no non-rollback action addresses the root, only the symptom. Downstream value risk: routing reads to replicas introduces replica lag into reporting and any reconciliation or balance-check path that silently reads those replicas, which in a payments system can produce wrong-but-plausible figures rather than visible errors, so I would scope the cut to analytics and dashboard queries only, exclude anything on the authorization or settlement decision path, and hold capacity and failover as the next-window options if write latency does not respond.
